title: Graph Beta: persist the current active graph projection
description: Graph Beta prerequisite for task-a9fd91c373c244c78df97945965a8038. Compose the landed @moe/core graph-revision lifecycle with SqliteEventStore so production code can answer “current graph snapshot for this project” from durable revision events. Measurement at HEAD a42ae2f1f9168d13b8b786404fc47b366cc8edd9: packages/core/src/planning/graph-revision-{contract,reducer}.ts exist; packages/store/src has zero GraphSnapshot/current-graph readers; apps/daemon only previews caller snapshots. This task owns the durable projection/read seam only. The daemon graph command/query transport is a separate consumer task. Stage: GRAPH BETA per the design’s incremental-delivery boundary. Not in scope: Foundation attempt ingress, launch templates, workspaces, fan-out dispatch, new runtime kinds, or edits to the authoritative design.
definitionOfDone: A focused production projection folds canonical graph-revision events per project and returns exactly one current ACTIVE revision as an immutable scheduler-compatible GraphSnapshot plus revision identity and graphEpoch provenance.

No active revision returns an exact stable UNKNOWN/not-found code and layer; corrupt, non-canonical, stale, or multiple-active histories fail closed under distinct stable code/layer mappings and yield no snapshot authority.

Projection replay is deterministic and order/identity checked: duplicate delivery is idempotent, conflicting bytes or impossible lifecycle ordering refuse, and raw event counts do not change on reads.

Focused tests use a real SqliteEventStore, assert exact refusal code and layer, prove generated hostile-case counts are nonzero, and include one accepted active-graph control read from production events rather than a helper reimplementation.

The task names the daemon graph transport task as its real consumer and records that task id in completion evidence; pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test reports a nonzero executed-test count and pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck exits 0 for owned paths.
taskRails: Use the existing @moe/core graph revision contracts/reducer and existing runtime graph vocabulary; do not mint command or query kinds.
Keep persistence, projection, and daemon transport concerns separate; this task does not wire HTTP/MCP or Foundation attempt ingress.
Fail closed with stable reason codes/layers and assert the reason code, layer, and nonzero generated-case count in every refusal sweep.
Use TDD; target <=250 physical lines per production source and split before 400; preserve foreign shared-tree work and commit only explicit owned paths.

THE NINE CASES, and what each is actually pinning:
1. put appends exactly ONE record keyed by the codec's own `graphContentHash` and returns it.
2. read returns bytes the REAL `decodeGraphContent` accepts, re-deriving the requested key. The decoder runs INSIDE the assertion because its digest check is the integrity authority — a remembered-bytes comparison would pass equally against a module that skipped the decode, which is exactly step 6's drill 2. Also asserts `snapshotIdentity !== graphContentHash`, pinning dec-64b2391c at this consumer.
3. CORRUPT ROW -> `GRAPH_CONTENT_DIGEST_MISMATCH` with `layer: GRAPH_BODY_RECORD_LAYER` and `sourceLayer: "GRAPH_CONTENT_IDENTITY"`. The fixture swaps the hash inside otherwise-canonical bytes; per the decoder's documented order (completion-reconcile -> digest -> re-encode) that is specifically DIGEST_MISMATCH and not the misleading NONCANONICAL, so the assertion pins the exact code rather than "refused".
4. ABSENT -> `GRAPH_BODY_ABSENT`, and explicitly asserts it is NOT the corruption code. Absence and corruption are distinct causes; collapsing them is what makes a later guard change invisible.
5. MISFILED -> `GRAPH_BODY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH`: perfectly canonical bytes stored under a key they do not hash to. This is the case a naive "decode succeeded, return it" implementation passes while returning content the caller never asked for.
6. UNENCODED WRITE -> `GRAPH_BODY_NOT_ENCODED`, and asserts NOTHING was appended. The fixture keeps the real hash and content but swaps `bytes` for a plausible hand-serialisation; accepting it would recreate the mint-your-own-identity seam the scheduler deliberately withholds.
7. IDEMPOTENCE: second put returns the same hash and the event count stays 1.
8. READ-ONLY on BOTH paths — accepted and refused — asserting counts before/after, since DoD 3 requires raw counts not to move on reads.
9. The refusal vocabulary is frozen and exhaustive, so step 6's drills can be checked against it; an unreachable code is as much a defect as a missing one.

DESIGN DECISION I MADE, worth QA's attention because it goes slightly beyond the plan's wording. The plan says to surface "the DECODER'S own code plus this module's layer". Taken literally that loses WHICH layer actually refused, which the epic rail explicitly requires when more than one layer can answer. So the refusal carries THREE fields: `code` (the decoder's own code when passing one through), `layer` (always `GRAPH_BODY_RECORD_LAYER` — who REPORTED), and `sourceLayer` (the decoder's own layer, or `null` when this module itself refused). Case 3 asserts all three; cases 4 and 5 assert `sourceLayer` is `null`. This satisfies the plan's intent and the rail's "which layer refused" without ambiguity.

A PLANTED ROW IS THE ONLY HONEST ROUTE TO THE DECODE GATE. `putGraphBody` only ever writes codec output, so a corrupt durable row is unreachable through the public write path by construction. The test therefore commits the damaged row directly under the module's own `graphBodyAggregateId(projectId, hash)` and `GRAPH_BODY_EVENT_TYPE` — both exported for exactly this reason — the same way a disk fault or hostile writer would (`mem:qa-planted-row-reaches-a-guard-no-honest-fixture-can`). Using the module's real aggregate deriver rather than a hand-built id also means a change to the keying scheme cannot silently orphan these tests.

implementationPlan.note:
STEP 3 — GREEN. `Test Files 1 passed (1) | Tests 9 passed (9)`, the same nine that failed to load in step 2. `graph-body-record.ts` is **191 physical lines**, inside the 250 target. The one-line bridge `graph-body-record.js` (`export * from "./graph-body-record.ts";`) matches the tracked convention in this package exactly (`activation-embargo.js`, `activation-ingress-contracts.js`, ...).

WHAT IT DOES, and the two places it deliberately does nothing:
- WRITE: refuses anything that is not codec output, then stores `content.bytes` VERBATIM under `graph-body:{projectId}:{graphContentHash}` with event type `GRAPH_BODY_RECORDED`. No hashing, no canonicalisation, no re-serialisation anywhere in the file — `encodeGraphContent` is the only lawful route to a `graphContentHash` and a second serialisation here would be a second identity for the same graph.
- READ: `decodeGraphContent` runs over the stored bytes BEFORE anything is returned, and its verdict is the authority. Accepted results are returned from `decoded.value`, not from the row — so a caller can never receive bytes the decoder did not just accept.

THE WRITE-SIDE CHECK IS A ROUND TRIP, NOT A SHAPE CHECK. `isCodecOutput` runs `decodeGraphContent(candidate.bytes)` and requires the decoded hash to equal the candidate's declared `graphContentHash`. A structural check (`has bytes`, `hash is hex64`) would accept the step-2 forgery, which carries a real hash and real content beside hand-serialised bytes. Only the codec can produce bytes that decode back to their own declared hash, so the round trip is what actually separates codec output from a lookalike.

THE POST-DECODE IDENTITY CHECK IS NOT REDUNDANT, and this is the subtle one. The decoder proves the bytes are SELF-CONSISTENT; it cannot know which key they were filed under. Bytes stored under someone else's key decode perfectly and would be returned as the answer to a question they do not answer (`mem:qa-decoded-success-is-not-the-answer-to-your-request`). So a successful decode whose `graphContentHash` differs from the requested key refuses `GRAPH_BODY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH` — step 2 case 5.

IDEMPOTENCE IS STRUCTURAL. Content-addressing means identical bytes cannot land under a different aggregate, so "already present" is by definition "the same bytes" and the second put returns without committing. This is a property of the keying rather than a check someone could forget to write.

REFUSAL VOCABULARY. Three own codes (`GRAPH_BODY_ABSENT`, `GRAPH_BODY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH`, `GRAPH_BODY_NOT_ENCODED`), frozen and asserted exhaustively by test 9. Codec codes pass through KEEPING THEIR OWN SPELLING and are not merged into this vocabulary — merging them would let a codec change silently widen this module's contract. `layer` is always `GRAPH_BODY_RECORD` (who reported); `sourceLayer` carries the codec's own layer on a passed-through verdict and `null` when the refusal originated here.

ONE DEFENSIVE BRANCH DISCLOSED HONESTLY: if the decoder ever refused with an EMPTY issues array, `decoded.issues[0]` is `undefined` and the code falls back to `GRAPH_BODY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH`. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` forces the branch to exist. I believe it is unreachable — every `refuse`/`passthrough` path in the codec emits at least one issue — so I am flagging it rather than claiming it is drilled; step 6's drills target reachable branches, and a drill on this one would be an equivalent-mutant exercise (`mem:qa-throw-probe-a-recorded-drill-names-an-unreachable-branch`).

4. SUPERSESSION — SUPERSEDED predecessor plus ACTIVE successor returns ONLY the successor, with `graphEpoch === predecessor.graphEpoch + 1` asserted RELATIVE to the predecessor's own state as well as to the literal 2. The epoch is a bound reference carried from the goal, never computed here.

Per revision aggregate: read events, hand the raw history to `replayGraphRevisionEvents`, and take the returned GraphRevisionState -- do NOT reimplement lifecycle, duplicate-delivery, ordering or identity rules locally; the core replay owns them and its refusal codes pass through with this module's layer attached. Select the single ACTIVE revision across the project's aggregates; more than one is the split-brain refusal, zero is not-found. Compose the step-3 body read for the ACTIVE revision's graphContentHash and return one frozen result: {content, snapshot fields, revisionId, graphEpoch, planHash, graphContentHash, snapshotIdentity, provenance naming the aggregate the epoch was bound from}. graphEpoch is a BOUND REFERENCE to the goal-owned epoch (contract's own comment) -- report it, never compute it. implementationPlan.note:
STEP 5 — GREEN. `Test Files 4 passed (4) | Tests 58 passed (58)` across `src/planning/` (my two suites plus the two pre-existing planning suites, all green). `npx tsc --project apps/daemon/tsconfig.json --noEmit` -> **EXIT 0**, zero diagnostics anywhere. Production line counts: `active-graph-projection.ts` **213**, `graph-body-record.ts` **191** — both inside the 250 target. `.js` bridge added to the tracked convention.

DELEGATION IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. Per aggregate the module reads events, hands the RAW history to `replayGraphRevisionEvents`, and takes the returned state. There is no local lifecycle table, no ordering comparison, no duplicate detection and no identity check anywhere in the file — the core owns all four, and its refusal `code` and `layer` pass straight through as `code` + `sourceLayer`. `graphEpoch` is copied from the replayed state and never computed, incremented or defaulted, because the contract says the goal is the only authority that advances an epoch.

ENUMERATION IS BY WRITTEN FACT, NOT BY GUESS. Aggregates are discovered by paging `readEventsByTypeAfter("GraphRevisionCreated", ...)` and collecting `aggregateId`, so discovery is bound to what was actually written rather than to a reconstructed id pattern. Paging follows `hasMore`/`nextCursor` rather than assuming one page.

A REFUSAL FROM ANY AGGREGATE STOPS THE WHOLE READ. This is a deliberate choice worth QA's attention: if one revision's history is unreadable, the project cannot honestly answer "the current graph", because the unreadable one might be the active one. Skipping it and answering from the rest would be the silent-authority failure this projection exists to prevent.

UNPARSEABLE PAYLOADS ARE PASSED THROUGH AS `null`, NOT FILTERED OUT. Dropping a corrupt row would hand the core a SHORTER but well-formed history, which could replay cleanly and yield a confident wrong answer. Passing `null` lets the core's own `EVENT_INVALID`/`HISTORY_INVALID` codes answer.

=== TWO TEST FAILURES ON FIRST RUN. BOTH WERE MY FIXTURES, NOT PRODUCTION. Recording them because each one would have been easy to "fix" by weakening the assertion. ===

(1) `fixture command rejected: REVISION_REBOUND` in the split-brain case. My approval/activation binding was a shared constant carrying `graphHash: PRIMARY.graphContentHash`, so the SECOND revision — created with the successor's hash — was being approved against the first revision's graph. The reducer was right to refuse. Fixed by deriving the binding from each revision's OWN content hash (`bindingOf(graphHash)`); the shared constant is gone. Had I instead relaxed the test, the split-brain case would have silently degraded into a one-active case and stopped testing split-brain at all.

(2) `duplicate create was accepted` in the hostile sweep. This one indicted the mutation, not the code: the core replay documents that a BYTE-IDENTICAL redelivery is idempotently IGNORED, so an appended identical create is legitimately accepted and still yields ACTIVE. My sweep had mis-classified correct, contract-mandated behaviour as hostile. The honest fix was not to delete the case but to MOVE it and invert it — there is now a dedicated test "is idempotent under byte-identical redelivery of the whole history" which re-delivers the entire generated history, asserts the projected answer is deep-equal to the first read, and asserts the RAW event count genuinely doubled while the answer did not move. That converts a wrong assertion into coverage of DoD 3's idempotence clause, which nothing else was pinning. The sweep's declared count moved 4 -> 3 and its `expect(cases.length).toBe(3)` guard moved with it, so the sweep still cannot silently shrink to zero.

NINE TESTS NOW, all with exact code/layer literals on refusal paths: accepted control (identity, epoch, provenance, frozen, `snapshotIdentity !== graphContentHash`), absent, split-brain, supersession successor at predecessor+1, core-replay passthrough naming `CORE_GRAPH_REVISION_REPLAY`, body-unavailable carrying `sourceCode: "GRAPH_BODY_ABSENT"`, read stability, idempotent redelivery, and the nonempty hostile sweep.

ONE DISCLOSURE ON FILE SIZE: the two TEST files are 284 and 483 lines. The epic rail's 250/400 cap is explicitly PER PRODUCTION SOURCE — the roster's own `isProductionModule` likewise excludes `.test.ts` — so these are compliant, and both production sources are well inside it. I am flagging the 483 rather than splitting it because a split would add a seventh file beyond the plan's declared owned paths, and the plan already carries a "touches 6 distinct files (target <=5)" size warning. If QA prefers the split, it is a mechanical extraction of the reducer-command fixtures.

implementationPlan.description: Mutation drills, three. Drill 1 (the ACTIVE selector is real): widen the projection's lifecycle filter to also accept APPROVED; the split-brain or not-found test must go RED on its code assertion. Drill 2 (the decode gate is load-bearing): make the body read return stored bytes without running decodeGraphContent; the corrupt-body test from step 2 must go RED. Drill 3 (delegation is real, not decorative): make the projection swallow the core replay's refusal and fold whatever partial state it can; the step-4 case (5) test must go RED on the core code assertion -- if it stays green, the test is not actually driving a corrupted history through the production path and must be strengthened. A drill that reddens by crashing or on a different assertion has not proven the binding. Restore by re-editing, never `git checkout` (destructive in the shared worktree), confirm `git diff --numstat` shows 0 added 0 deleted per drilled file, one drill at a time -- a peer commit landing mid-drill can swallow the patch and leave git reading clean.
implementationPlan.note:
STEP 6 — THREE DRILLS RUN, ONE AT A TIME. Two proved their binding immediately; ONE SURVIVED and exposed a real coverage hole, and one reddened for the WRONG REASON and had to be rewritten. Final state: all production files byte-identical to their pre-drill baseline, `Test Files 4 passed (4) | Tests 59 passed (59)`.

RESTORE ANCHOR IS A HASH, NOT GIT. All six deliverables are UNTRACKED (`git status` shows `??`), so `git checkout`/`git diff --numstat` cannot restore or verify them — a `--numstat` check would read clean no matter what I did (`mem:untracked-deliverable-cannot-be-drill-restored-by-git`). I snapshotted `sha256sum` of both production sources before drilling and diffed against it after each revert. Final `diff` of the baseline vs post-drill hashes: IDENTICAL for both files.

=== DRILL 1 (the ACTIVE selector is real) — SURVIVED FIRST, THEN KILLED ===
Widened `lifecycle === "ACTIVE"` to also accept `"APPROVED"`. Result: **10 passed, ZERO red.** A surviving mutant, and the diagnosis was a genuine gap rather than an equivalent mutant: every fixture reached ACTIVE through the COMPOUND `graph.approve` command (approval+activation in one), so no history in the suite ever rested in APPROVED. The widened filter had nothing to observe. My "absent" case used a DRAFT-only history, which the mutation does not touch.
FIX — strengthened the test, did not weaken the drill. Added `approveOnlyOf()` (approval WITHOUT activation, landing the revision in APPROVED) and a new case: "treats an APPROVED revision as NOT active, even with its body stored". It asserts `lifecycle === "APPROVED"` and `graphEpoch === 0` on the fixture itself, and stores the body, so nothing but the lifecycle filter can explain the refusal.
RE-RUN: base green at 11 -> drill re-applied -> **1 failed | 10 passed**, failing exactly the new APPROVED test. Binding proven.

=== DRILL 2 (the decode gate is load-bearing) — FIRST ATTEMPT INVALID, REDONE ===
First attempt neutered the failure branch with `if (false)`. It reddened the right test, but with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'graphContentHash')` at `graph-body-record.ts:181` — a CRASH, not a verdict. Per the plan's own rule ("a drill that reddens by crashing or on a different assertion has not proven the binding"), I discarded it rather than banking a red that only proved a refusal object has no `.value`.
DRILL 2b, the realistic defect: on decode failure, TRUST THE DURABLE ROW — return `row.payload` with the content JSON-parsed straight out of the stored bytes. That is what "skip the decode gate" actually looks like when someone writes it deliberately, and it returns a coherent value instead of crashing.
RESULT: **`AssertionError: expected true to be false`** on the corrupt-row test's `expect(read.ok).toBe(false)` — the tampered row was ACCEPTED. Clean assertion failure on the intended test. The decode gate is load-bearing.

=== DRILL 3 (delegation is real, not decorative) — KILLED FIRST TRY ===
Made the projection swallow the core replay's refusal (`continue` instead of propagating), so a project holding one unreplayable revision quietly answers from the rest.
RESULT: **`expected 'ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT' to be 'GRAPH_REVISION_REPLAY_IDENTITY_CONFLICT'`** on the passthrough test — red on the CODE assertion specifically, which is the assertion that matters. This is the one the plan flagged as the tell: had it stayed green, my test would not really have been driving a corrupted history through the production path. It does. Delegation is observable, and the core's own code genuinely reaches the caller.

WHY THE SURVIVING MUTANT IS THE MOST VALUABLE RESULT HERE. Drill 1's survival was not a false alarm and not an equivalent mutant — the projection's exclusion of APPROVED was completely untested, and the whole suite would have stayed green if someone had widened that filter in a later refactor. The suite went 10 tests -> 11, and the new case is the only thing in the repo pinning "APPROVED is not ACTIVE" for this reader. `mem:qa-drill-the-flag-not-just-the-guard` applies: a drill that survives is information, and the correct response is a stronger test, never a softer drill.

DISCIPLINE: one drill at a time; each reverted and hash-verified against baseline before the next was applied; no `git checkout`, no stash, no reset (the tree also holds untracked peer work under `apps/daemon/src/projections/`). The only file changed by this step is the projection TEST file, which gained `approveOnlyOf` and the APPROVED case.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered: I drafted a plan for this task once before (ownership refused the submission -- it belonged to architect-f956ffe1 then), and this replan is BETTER than that draft in three specific ways because the producers have since landed. (1) The old draft had the body record canonicalise and hash the snapshot itself; that is now forbidden and unnecessary -- encodeGraphContent is the only lawful route to a graphContentHash (the scheduler root comment says exactly this and withholds the raw mechanics), so the body record stores the codec's canonical BYTES and the read side re-validates through decodeGraphContent, whose digest check is the integrity authority. (2) The old draft had the projection fold lifecycle events with locally-enforced ordering/duplicate rules; task-ee27ed7c landed replayGraphRevisionEvents with snapshotted input, idempotent redelivery, identity-conflict refusal and no-partial-state -- so the projection DELEGATES and surfaces core codes rather than reimplementing rules, which also kills a whole class of drift. (3) The old draft could not name the structural/content identity split; now the result carries BOTH graphContentHash and snapshotIdentity and the accepted control asserts they differ, pinning dec-64b2391c at the consumer. REJECTED: (a) storing decoded content JSON instead of canonical bytes -- a second serialisation invites a second identity; (b) accepting raw content fields at putGraphBody -- recreates the mint-your-own-hash seam; (c) a single combined module -- body record and lifecycle fold have separate refusal vocabularies and would breach the per-file line target; (d) waiting for a durable graph-revision event writer -- none exists in production yet, and this task's contract is the read/persist seam; tests seed through reduceGraphRevision, the same way the replay surface's own suite does.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights: Measured at HEAD 8222b9e. REPLAY: packages/core/src/planning/graph-revision-replay.ts:211 replayGraphRevisionEvents(history: unknown) -> GraphRevisionReplayResult; root-exported at packages/core/src/index.ts:109 with GRAPH_REVISION_REPLAY_CODES and result types; admissible() enforces exact event keys per kind; byte-identical redelivery ignored; same-version-different-bytes -> GRAPH_REVISION_REPLAY_IDENTITY_CONFLICT; missing create -> GRAPH_REVISION_REPLAY_MISSING_CREATE; refusals carry code+layer, never partial state. CONTENT: packages/scheduler root exports encodeGraphContent(content, policyOverride?) and decodeGraphContent(input) (index.ts:90-91); GraphContent = {schemaVersion, graphContentHash (all seven design-197 fields, lowercase hex64 -- the spelling @moe/core's revision gate requires), snapshotIdentity (structure-only, documented never equal), content: GraphRevisionContent, bytes}; decodeGraphContent refuses GRAPH_CONTENT_NOT_BYTES / TOO_LARGE / digest mismatch etc. from the frozen GRAPH_CONTENT_ISSUE_CODES over three frozen layers. GraphRevisionState (core contract :122) carries boundHashes/goalRef/graphContentHash/graphEpoch/lifecycle/planHash/revisionId/submissionRef/version; graphEpoch is a bound reference to the goal-owned epoch -- report, never compute. NOTHING writes graph-revision events in production yet (grep: zero non-test writers), so tests seed via reduceGraphRevision. apps/daemon/src/planning/ already exists (approval-activation, approval-gate, planning-services) -- the new modules sit beside them. apps/daemon/package.json already declares @moe/core, @moe/scheduler, @moe/store; step 1 still proves the edges with a compiled bare-specifier probe because a manifest line is not a resolution proof. A new .ts module needs its one-line .js bridge.
planningNotes.risks: The load-bearing risk is identity theatre: a projection that returns content whose hash was never re-checked is authority-shaped without being authoritative. The design here routes ALL integrity through decodeGraphContent -- drill 2 proves the gate is load-bearing, and the accepted control asserts graphContentHash !== snapshotIdentity so the two-hash confusion (the exact failure dec-64b2391c was raised to prevent, still easy because a structural value once wore the content name) cannot re-enter through this consumer. Second, split-brain: two ACTIVE revisions must refuse, never disambiguate by epoch or recency -- picking a winner grants authority during precisely the condition the projection exists to detect. Third, silent local lifecycle rules: if the projection reimplements ordering/duplicate handling instead of delegating to replayGraphRevisionEvents, the two drift and the tests police the copy; drill 3 forces the delegation to be real. Fourth, hand-written event literals in tests let the projection pass against shapes production never writes -- seed through reduceGraphRevision only. Fifth, distinct causes need distinct codes: no-active, multiple-active, replay-refused, body-absent, body-corrupt are five failures; collapsing any two makes a later guard change invisible. Sixth, close every store handle on every path including refusals; a held SQLite handle kills the vitest worker. Seventh, consumers (c4b80778, eacea969, 32c1ba45) are all BLOCKED -- name them as the consumer edge honestly rather than implying a live call site. Finally, the shared worktree rules: restore drills by re-editing, commit by explicit pathspec only.
